question: Why is the Moon becoming a strategic prize, where are its resources, and who is racing to reach them?

key_changes_found_in_2026: Artemis II flew around the Moon in April 2026 (splashdown 10 April).
Artemis III became a 2027 crewed test flight in low Earth orbit; first landing moved to Artemis IV in 2028.
NASA announced a south-pole Moon Base at its 'Ignition' event on 24 March 2026 (phases: to 2029, 2029-2032, from 2032).
Chang'e-7 did not launch in its August 2026 window; delayed to 2027. Target near Shackleton crater (88.8 S, 123.4 E).
Chang'e-8 payloads may move to a 2030/31 timeline after China merged its robotic and crewed lunar programs.
Russia pushed Luna-26 to 2028, Luna-27A (south pole) to 2029, Luna-27B (north pole) to 2030, Luna-28 to 2036.
Griffin-1 now targets January 2027; every other U.S. CLPS lander slipped to 2027.
Artemis Accords reached 78 signatories on 28 October 2026 (Vietnam). ILRS: 13 countries as tracked mid-2026.
India chose site MM-4 near Mons Mouton for Chandrayaan-4 (2028).
South Korea named six candidate sites for its 2032 lander (25 March 2026).

helium3_facts.earth_reserves: less than 10 kg (about 5 parts per trillion) - Nature Comms Earth & Env 2024
helium3_facts.moon_soil: 3.7 ppb highlands, 7.8 ppb maria (conservative); Apollo 11 sample 10084 averaged 11.8 ppb; some soils ~20 ppb
helium3_facts.total_on_moon: at least 1 million t (CNSA); about 2.47 million t (LPSC 2007 estimate)
helium3_facts.soil_per_kg: 100,000 to 1,000,000 t of regolith per kg (USGS, via SpaceNews)
helium3_facts.excavator_rate: about 100 t of regolith per hour (Interlune/Vermeer prototype)
helium3_facts.price: ~$2,500 per liter; ~$20M per kg; ~7,400 liters per kg
helium3_facts.deals: Bluefors up to 10,000 L/yr 2028-2037 (>$300M); Maybell Quantum multi-year; DOE 3 L by April 2029
